blocks.text: [II, 735] In Tobit the Latin copy disagrees with the Greek on this word, Tob. II, 9. (var. 11.). For in the Greek Tobit says, Καὶ οὐκ ᾔδειν ὅτι στρουθία ἐν τῷ τοίχῳ ἐστί· καὶ, τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν μου ἀνεωγότων, ἀφώδευσαν τὰ στρουθία θερμὸν εἰς τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς μου [Kai ouk ēdein hoti strouthia en tō toichō esti; kai, tōn ophthalmōn mou aneōgotōn, aphōdeusan ta strouthia thermon eis tous ophthalmous mou]; And I did not know that there were sparrows in the wall; and, my eyes being open, the sparrows voided warm dung into my eyes. But the Latin relates that it happened one day that, when Tobit had fallen asleep beside a wall, warm dung fell upon him as he slept from a swallows' nest. I do not see how these can be reconciled otherwise than by saying that στρουθία [strouthia] in the Greek there are not sparrows but little birds, just as Moschopulus and Phavorinus asserted above that every kind of little bird is called στρουθία [strouthia] in Greek. Or else that by the name of sparrows swallows are meant, after the manner of the Arabs, who call the swallow عصفور الجنة [ʿuṣfūr al-janna] the sparrow of Paradise. Similar is the case of Prov. XXVI, 2., where some render the Hebrew דרור deror as swallow, but the Greek interpreters as στρουθοὺς [strouthous], sparrows.
